# Second Question: ANOVA

## Data preparation

```{r setup, echo = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

# Import dataset
data <- read.csv("bodyPerformance.csv")

# Creating age categories
data$age_cat <- cut(
  data$age,
  breaks = c(0, 30, 40, 50, Inf),
  labels = c("<30", "30-39", "40-49", "50+"),
  right = FALSE
)

# Convert categorical variables to factors
data$class <- factor(data$class,
                     levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
data$gender <- factor(data$gender)

# Check data structure
str(data)
```

## Task 2(a): Check the distribution of the variables body fat (%), diastolic blood pressure, number of sit-ups and broad jump distance (cm) for each age group and performance class.

First, we prepare the four numerical variables to analyze their distributions.

```{r}
# Prepare data for distribution analysis
q2_data <- data %>%
  select(age_cat, class, body.fat_., diastolic,
         sit.ups.counts, broad.jump_cm) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(body.fat_., diastolic,
             sit.ups.counts, broad.jump_cm),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Check the resulting structure
head(q2_data)
```

### Distribution by age group

We use histograms to examine the shape of the distributions for each age group.

```{r}

ggplot(q2_data, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable + age_cat, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of variables by age group",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Frequency"
  )

```

We also use boxplots to identify differences in central tendency, variability and potential outliers.

```{r}
ggplot(q2_data, aes(x = age_cat, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "steelblue",
    outlier.color = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Variables by age group",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Value"
  )
```

### Distribution by performance class

We repeat the analysis for the four performance classes (A, B, C and D).

```{r}

ggplot(q2_data, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable + class, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of variables by performance class",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Frequency"
  )

```

```{r}
ggplot(q2_data, aes(x = class, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "steelblue",
    outlier.color = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Variables by performance class",
    x = "Performance class",
    y = "Value"
  )
```

### Descriptive statistics

```{r}
# Descriptive statistics by age group
q2_data %>%
  group_by(variable, age_cat) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(value)),
    mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd = round(sd(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Descriptive statistics by performance class
q2_data %>%
  group_by(variable, class) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(value)),
    mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd = round(sd(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Interpretation

The distributions of body fat percentage, diastolic blood pressure, sit-up counts, and broad jump distance were examined across age groups and performance classes using histograms and boxplots (Figures 1–2 and Appendix Figures A1–A2).

Age groups. Figure 1 shows that body fat percentage tends to increase with age, with mean values ranging from 21.83% for individuals under 30 to 26.29% for those aged 50 and above. Conversely, mean broad jump distance decreases from 202.20 to 158.54 cm, while mean sit-up counts decrease from 46.12 to 26.82. Diastolic blood pressure varies less substantially, ranging from 76.66 to 81.28 mmHg across age groups.

Performance classes. Figure 2 indicates that lower performance classes are associated with higher body fat percentages and reduced physical performance. Mean body fat increases from 20.54% in class A to 27.74% in class D, while mean broad jump distance decreases from 202.74 to 173.82 cm and mean sit-up counts from 47.85 to 29.88. Diastolic blood pressure exhibits smaller differences between classes.

The histograms (Appendix Figures A1–A2) reveal approximately unimodal distributions for several variables, although some skewness and deviations from normality are observed. The boxplots also identify potential outliers, particularly in body fat and diastolic blood pressure.

These descriptive findings will be further investigated through inferential statistical analysis in Section 2(b).

## Task 2(b): ANOVA

## Diastolic blood pressure by age group

```{r}
# Remove invalid diastolic blood pressure values
diastolic_data <- data %>%
  filter(diastolic > 0, !is.na(age_cat))

# One-way ANOVA
model_diastolic_age <- aov(
  diastolic ~ age_cat,
  data = diastolic_data
)

# ANOVA results
summary(model_diastolic_age)
```

```{r}
# Test homogeneity of variances
library(car)

leveneTest(diastolic ~ age_cat,
           data = diastolic_data)
```


```{r}
# Normality of ANOVA residuals

# Extract residuals
res <- residuals(model_diastolic_age)

# Shapiro-Wilk test (maximum 5000 observations)
set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(res, 5000))

# Q-Q plot
qqnorm(res, main = "Q-Q Plot: Diastolic BP by Age")
qqline(res, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```


```{r}

# Examine extreme diastolic blood pressure values

summary(diastolic_data$diastolic)

# Lowest observations
diastolic_data %>%
  arrange(diastolic) %>%
  select(age, gender, diastolic, age_cat) %>%
  head(10)

# Highest observations
diastolic_data %>%
  arrange(desc(diastolic)) %>%
  select(age, gender, diastolic, age_cat) %>%
  head(10)

```


```{r}
# Remove clearly implausible observations
diastolic_clean <- diastolic_data %>%
  filter(!diastolic %in% c(6, 8))

# Number of removed observations
nrow(diastolic_data) - nrow(diastolic_clean)

# Refit ANOVA
model_diastolic_age_clean <- aov(
  diastolic ~ age_cat,
  data = diastolic_clean
)

summary(model_diastolic_age_clean)

# Check homogeneity of variances
leveneTest(diastolic ~ age_cat,
           data = diastolic_clean)

# Check normality of residuals
res_clean <- residuals(model_diastolic_age_clean)

set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(res_clean, 5000))

# Q-Q plot
qqnorm(res_clean, main = "Q-Q Plot: Cleaned Diastolic BP")
qqline(res_clean, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}


# Post hoc comparisons: Tukey HSD
tukey_diastolic_age <- TukeyHSD(
  model_diastolic_age_clean,
  "age_cat"
)

tukey_diastolic_age


```


```{r}
# Post hoc comparisons: Bonferroni correction
bonferroni_diastolic_age <- with(
  diastolic_clean,
  pairwise.t.test(
    diastolic,
    age_cat,
    p.adjust.method = "bonferroni"
  )
)

bonferroni_diastolic_age
```


```{r}
# Post hoc comparisons: Fisher's LSD test

library(agricolae)

lsd_diastolic_age <- LSD.test(
  model_diastolic_age_clean,
  "age_cat",
  p.adj = "none",
  group = FALSE
)

lsd_diastolic_age$comparison
```

# Body fat (%) by age group

```{r}
# Prepare body fat data

  filter(!is.na(body.fat_.), !is.na(age_cat))

  data = bodyfat_data
)

# Homogeneity of variances

  body.fat_. ~ age_cat,
  data = bodyfat_data
)

  body.fat_. ~ age_cat,
  data = bodyfat_data,
  var.equal = FALSE
)

welch_bodyfat_age

```



```{r}
# Normality of body fat distributions by age group

res_bodyfat_age <- residuals(model_bodyfat_age)

set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(res_bodyfat_age, 5000))

# Q-Q plots for each age group
ggplot(bodyfat_data, aes(sample = body.fat_.)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ age_cat, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Q-Q Plots: Body Fat by Age Group",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  )
```


```{r}
# Post hoc comparisons: Tukey HSD

)

tukey_bodyfat_age

  bodyfat_data,
  pairwise.t.test(
    body.fat_.,
    age_cat,
    p.adjust.method = "bonferroni"
  )
)

bonferroni_bodyfat_age


# Post hoc comparisons: Fisher's LSD

```

--- Encara he de revisar o modificar el texte més ---

One-way ANOVA was performed to examine the association of age group and performance class with diastolic blood pressure, body fat percentage, sit-up counts, and broad jump distance. For each variable, the two factors were analyzed separately. Statistical significance was assessed at α = 0.05.

Before interpreting the results, the ANOVA assumptions were evaluated using Levene's test for homogeneity of variances, Shapiro-Wilk for residual normality, and Q-Q plots. All eight models showed statistically significant differences between groups (p < 0.001).

### Diastolic blood pressure

Diastolic blood pressure differed significantly across both age groups (F(3, 13386) = 150.4, p < 0.001, η² = 0.033) and performance classes (F(3, 13386) = 25.22, p < 0.001, η² = 0.006). Levene's test did not reject homogeneity of variances for either factor (p = 0.101 and p = 0.121, respectively). Shapiro-Wilk rejected residual normality, although the Q-Q plots showed approximately linear patterns with deviations mainly in the tails.

For age groups, Tukey HSD and Bonferroni identified five significant pairwise differences, with the only non-significant comparison occurring between 40–49 and 50+ years. Fisher's LSD additionally identified this comparison as significant (p = 0.015). For performance classes, Tukey and Bonferroni identified four significant comparisons (A–B, A–D, B–D and C–D), whereas LSD additionally identified A–C.

Overall, diastolic blood pressure showed statistically significant but relatively small differences between groups.

### Body fat percentage

Body fat percentage differed significantly across age groups (F(3, 13389) = 294.9, p < 0.001, η² = 0.062) and performance classes (F(3, 13389) = 721.2, p < 0.001, η² = 0.139). Levene's test indicated heterogeneous variances in both analyses (p < 0.001), while Shapiro-Wilk rejected normality. However, the Q-Q plots showed an approximately linear pattern in their central regions.

For age groups, Tukey and Bonferroni identified five significant pairwise differences, except between individuals under 30 and those aged 30–39. LSD additionally identified this comparison as significant (p = 0.011). For performance classes, all three post hoc methods identified significant differences between all six pairs.

Mean body fat percentage increased from 21.83% to 26.29% across the youngest and oldest age groups, and from 20.54% in class A to 27.74% in class D.

### Number of sit-ups

The number of sit-ups differed significantly across age groups (F(3, 13389) ≈ 1893, p < 0.001, η² = 0.298) and performance classes (F(3, 13389) ≈ 1197, p < 0.001, η² = 0.211). Both Levene's and Shapiro-Wilk tests were significant (p < 0.001), indicating deviations from homogeneity of variances and residual normality. The Q-Q plots showed an approximately linear central region, with more pronounced deviations in the tails.

Tukey HSD, Bonferroni and Fisher's LSD identified significant differences between all six pairs of age groups and all six pairs of performance classes (all p < 0.001).

Mean sit-up counts decreased from 46.12 in individuals under 30 to 26.82 in those aged 50 and above. Similarly, mean performance decreased from 47.85 sit-ups in class A to 29.88 in class D.

### Broad jump distance

Broad jump distance differed significantly across age groups (F(3, 13379) ≈ 1165, p < 0.001, η² ≈ 0.207) and performance classes (F(3, 13379) = 340.4, p < 0.001, η² ≈ 0.071). Ten observations with zero jump distance were excluded in a sensitivity analysis, without materially changing the ANOVA conclusions.

Levene's test indicated heterogeneous variances for both factors (p = 0.0025 for age and p < 0.001 for class). Shapiro-Wilk also rejected residual normality (p < 0.001), with the Q-Q plots showing deviations particularly in the tails.

For age groups, all three post hoc methods identified five significant comparisons. The only non-significant difference was between individuals under 30 and those aged 30–39. For performance classes, all three methods identified significant differences between all six pairs (p < 0.001).

Broad jump distance decreased substantially in older age groups and lower performance classes, with the largest class difference observed between A and D (28.61 cm).

### Overall interpretation

The results indicate significant associations between age, performance class and all four measurements. Age showed the strongest association with sit-up counts (η² = 0.298) and broad jump distance (η² ≈ 0.207), whereas performance class showed substantial associations with sit-up counts (η² = 0.211) and body fat percentage (η² = 0.139).

Tukey HSD and Bonferroni provided consistent significance decisions across all analyses. Fisher's LSD identified three additional significant comparisons, reflecting its less conservative approach to multiple testing.

Although the large sample sizes provide some robustness against moderate departures from normality, several models violated the homogeneity and normality assumptions. Consequently, the classical ANOVA and post hoc results should be interpreted cautiously. Independence of observations must also be supported by the data collection design. Finally, the observed associations should not be interpreted as causal effects, particularly because performance class is derived from physical performance measurements.



## Task 2(c): Two-way ANOVA


```{r}
# Sit-ups by age group and gender
model_situps_two_way <- aov(
  sit.ups.counts ~ age_cat * gender,
  data = situps_data
)

summary(model_situps_two_way)
```

```{r}

# Interaction plot: Age group and Gender

interaction.plot(
  x.factor = situps_data$age_cat,
  trace.factor = situps_data$gender,
  response = situps_data$sit.ups.counts,
  fun = mean,
  type = "b",
  col = c("blue", "red"),
  pch = c(16, 17),
  xlab = "Age group",
  ylab = "Mean number of sit-ups",
  trace.label = "Gender",
  main = "Interaction between Age and Gender on Sit-ups"
)
```


```{r}

# Check assumptions: Sit-ups Two-way ANOVA

# Normality of residuals
res_situps_two_way <- residuals(model_situps_two_way)

set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(res_situps_two_way, 5000))

# Q-Q plot
qqnorm(res_situps_two_way,
       main = "Q-Q Plot: Sit-ups Two-way ANOVA")
qqline(res_situps_two_way, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Homogeneity of variances across age-gender groups
situps_data$age_gender <- interaction(
  situps_data$age_cat,
  situps_data$gender
)

leveneTest(
  sit.ups.counts ~ age_gender,
  data = situps_data
)

```

```{r}

# Broad jump by age group and gender

model_jump_two_way <- aov(
  broad.jump_cm ~ age_cat * gender,
  data = jump_clean
)

summary(model_jump_two_way)

```

```{r}

# Interaction plot: Age group and Gender

interaction.plot(
  x.factor = jump_clean$age_cat,
  trace.factor = jump_clean$gender,
  response = jump_clean$broad.jump_cm,
  fun = mean,
  type = "b",
  col = c("blue", "red"),
  pch = c(16, 17),
  xlab = "Age group",
  ylab = "Mean broad jump distance (cm)",
  trace.label = "Gender",
  main = "Interaction between Age and Gender on Broad Jump"
)

```

```{r}

# Check assumptions: Broad Jump Two-way ANOVA

# Normality of residuals
res_jump_two_way <- residuals(model_jump_two_way)

set.seed(123)
shapiro.test(sample(res_jump_two_way, 5000))

# Q-Q plot
qqnorm(res_jump_two_way,
       main = "Q-Q Plot: Broad Jump Two-way ANOVA")
qqline(res_jump_two_way, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Homogeneity of variances
jump_clean$age_gender <- interaction(
  jump_clean$age_cat,
  jump_clean$gender
)

leveneTest(
  broad.jump_cm ~ age_gender,
  data = jump_clean
)

```

A two-way ANOVA was performed to investigate the combined effects of age group and gender on sit-up counts and broad jump distance, including their interaction.

For **sit-up performance**, both age group ($F(3,13385)=2591.19$) and gender ($F(1,13385)=4868.91$) were statistically significant ($p<0.001$). Their interaction was also significant ($F(3,13385)=25.58$, $p<0.001$), although its effect size was small ($\eta_p^2\approx0.006$). (Ficar alguna referència a figura) Mean sit-up counts decrease with age for both genders, with males consistently outperforming females. The non-parallel trends indicate that the relationship between age and sit-up performance varies by gender.

For **broad jump distance**, age group ($F(3,13375)=2683.04$), gender ($F(1,13375)=17406.56$), and their interaction ($F(3,13375)=9.60$) were also statistically significant (all $p<0.001$). However, the interaction effect was small ($\eta_p^2\approx0.002$). (Ficar alguna referència a figura) Jump distance decreases with age in both genders, with males consistently achieving greater distances. The slightly different trends across age groups support the presence of a significant interaction.

Regarding **ANOVA assumptions**, Shapiro--Wilk tests rejected residual normality for both sit-ups ($W=0.9912$) and broad jump ($W=0.9837$), with $p<0.001$ in both cases. Similarly, Levene's tests indicated heterogeneous variances across age--gender groups (both $p<0.001$). The Q-Q plots showed approximately linear central regions but deviations in the tails. Therefore, despite the large sample size, the ANOVA results should be interpreted cautiously. Independence of observations was assumed but could not be verified from the available data.

Overall, age and gender were significantly associated with both physical performance measures. Although their interactions were statistically significant, their small effect sizes suggest that the differences in age-related performance patterns between genders were relatively modest.
